title: The Actuary Who Failed: Rahway, Hyde Park, Santiago, Russian Hill
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: A New Jersey Town and a Scholarship

stops.name: East New York, Brooklyn, the birth
stops.date_confidence: attested for city and date (Wikipedia, Milton Friedman; Hoover/OAC finding aid chronology, which opens at 1912). The street address 502 Barbey Street comes only from a biographical reconstruction on Libertarianism.org that was not independently fetched, and the coordinate is therefore an East New York pin rather than a house.
stops.campa: Sarah Ethel Landau and Jeno Saul Friedman, both born in Beregszasz in Carpathian Ruthenia and both emigrated young, are living in East New York when their fourth child and only son is born. The neighborhood is poor, crowded and Jewish, a first landing place rather than a settled one. Family reconstruction puts the house on Barbey Street, though no document reached here fixes the address. The father will be dead before the boy finishes high school. There is no money in this household now and there will be none for the whole of his childhood.
suggested_refs: The Hoover Institution finding aid to the Milton Friedman papers, 1931-2006, whose life chronology begins with this date
sources: Online Archive of California, finding aid to the Milton Friedman papers 1931-2006 (oac.cdlib.org)

stops.name: Rahway, New Jersey, the family moves out of the city
stops.date_confidence: attested that the family moved to Rahway when he was about thirteen months old (Wikipedia, Milton Friedman); the month is not established, so the date is set to January to order the segment. Coordinates are the town center, not a house.
stops.campa: At about thirteen months the family leaves Brooklyn for Rahway, a small manufacturing town in Union County twenty miles down the road. He grows up there rather than in the city, and the move fixes the whole geography of his childhood: one town, one school system, one set of streets. Money is short in the household the entire time he is in it, which is how he first meets the American economy, years before he has a name for any part of it. He will live in Rahway for the next fifteen years.
suggested_refs: Rahway, Union County, New Jersey, the town of the whole childhood

stops.name: Rahway High School, the diploma at fifteen
stops.date_confidence: attested that he graduated in 1928 shortly before his sixteenth birthday (Wikipedia, Milton Friedman); the exact day is not established and June is used to order the segment. Coordinates are the Madison Avenue school building given in Wikipedia's Rahway High School article, which is not certainly the 1928 building. His father's death year is contradicted between genealogical sources: 1 November 1927 in one, 1929 in another. The contradiction is left open.
stops.campa: He finishes the course before his sixteenth birthday, the first of the family headed for a university. His mother keeps the household going; a competitive state scholarship, not the family, will pay for what comes next, and he knows it before he leaves the building. His father dies in the same stretch of months, and the family reconstructions do not agree whether the year was 1927 or 1929. Whether the boy holding that diploma is newly fatherless or about to be is not something the surviving record settles.
suggested_refs: Rahway High School, 1012 Madison Avenue, Rahway, Union County, New Jersey

stops.name: Rutgers University, the actuary who failed
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1928-1932 at Rutgers and for the B.A. in mathematics and economics (Wikipedia; Econlib biography; Hoover/OAC finding aid). Month set to September to order the segment. Coordinates are Old Queens on the College Avenue campus, per Wikipedia's Rutgers article.
stops.campa: On a competitive scholarship he enters Rutgers intending to become an actuary, a trade that pays and asks nothing but mathematics. He works to cover what the scholarship does not, sits the actuarial examinations, and passes some and fails others. The degree comes in 1932, in mathematics and economics both, into the worst labor market the country has. Two teachers have turned him by then: Arthur Burns, who shows him what empirical research actually is, and Homer Jones, who tells him the live work is in economics and that Chicago is where to go and do it.
suggested_refs: Old Queens and the College Avenue campus, Rutgers University, New Brunswick

stops.name: University of Chicago, the alphabetical seating
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1932 arrival, the 1933 M.A., and the alphabetical seating that put him beside Rose Director (Wikipedia, Milton Friedman; the M.A. year is confirmed independently by the Hoover/OAC chronology). Month set to September to order the segment.
stops.campa: A tuition scholarship carries him to Hyde Park in the pit of the Depression, the hardest financial year he will ever have. He takes price theory from Jacob Viner and studies under Frank Knight, Henry Schultz and Henry Simons. In one economics course the seats are assigned alphabetically, and Director, Rose, is placed beside Friedman, Milton. She is a graduate student in economics in her own right and the sister of Aaron Director. They will marry six years from now and stay married sixty-eight years, and half the books that carry his name will pass through her hands first. The master's degree comes in 1933.
suggested_refs: The Chicago economics department of Viner, Knight, Schultz and Simons, the school before it was called one
sources: Online Archive of California, finding aid to the Milton Friedman papers 1931-2006

stops.name: Columbia University, the fellowship year
stops.date_confidence: attested as the 1933-1934 academic year (Wikipedia, Milton Friedman, which dates the Columbia fellowship 1933-1934). The verified pool's chronology lens had dated this to 1934, which pushes it a year late and collides with the Schultz assistantship; the earlier date is followed here and the discrepancy is recorded rather than buried.
stops.campa: A fellowship takes him from Hyde Park to Morningside Heights for one academic year. Harold Hotelling gives him mathematical statistics at a level Chicago did not. From Wesley Clair Mitchell he takes the National Bureau habit: business cycles counted before they are explained, institutions described before they are modeled. He arrives holding Chicago price theory and leaves holding both, which is the equipment he works with for the next fifty years. The year buys him no degree and no post, and in the autumn he goes back to Chicago as somebody's assistant.
suggested_refs: Wesley Clair Mitchell's National Bureau method, which Friedman carried out of Columbia and used for the rest of his life

stops.name: University of Chicago, research assistant to Henry Schultz
stops.date_confidence: attested as 1934-1935 (Wikipedia, Milton Friedman). The verified pool cited the Hoover/OAC finding aid for this, wrongly: that chronology has eleven entries and does not mention Schultz at all. The correction is recorded here.
stops.campa: He comes back to Chicago as research assistant to Henry Schultz, who is fitting statistical demand curves to American agriculture. The work itself is arithmetic. What he gets out of the year is the room: George Stigler and W. Allen Wallis are in the same cohort, and for the next fifty years the three of them will pass each other jobs, arguments, manuscripts and introductions. There is no faculty position at the end of it. In 1935 there is no faculty position anywhere.
suggested_refs: Henry Schultz, The Theory and Measurement of Demand, the project Friedman assisted on

stops.name: Washington, the National Resources Committee budget study
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1935 and for the consumer budget work (Hoover/OAC finding aid; Wikipedia). Month set to September to order the segment; the Committee's office building is not established, so the coordinate is central Washington.
stops.campa: No university is hiring, so Wallis brings him into the New Deal instead: the National Resources Committee, and a consumer purchase study covering thousands of American households, income set against expenditure item by item. He is twenty-three and handling the largest budget survey yet assembled in the country; those households will feed the permanent income hypothesis two decades later. He says afterward that the emergency employment programs were right for the emergency and that the price and wage controls were not. He is drawing a federal salary the whole time he is saying it.
suggested_refs: The 1935-1936 Study of Consumer Purchases, the data behind A Theory of the Consumption Function
sources: Online Archive of California, finding aid to the Milton Friedman papers 1931-2006

stops.name: New York, the National Bureau and the marriage
stops.date_confidence: attested that he joined the NBER research staff in 1937 and stayed affiliated until 1981 (Wikipedia; Hoover/OAC finding aid, which gives lecturer dates 1937-1940). The marriage year is contradicted in the sources: Wikipedia's infobox says 1936, while its own article body, the Hoover/OAC chronology and Simple Wikipedia all say 1938. The three-source figure of 1938 is followed. No source reached names the city of the ceremony, so it is placed at his workplace of the period and the location is left unestablished. The NBER's exact New York address was not pinned down; the coordinate is midtown Manhattan.
stops.campa: He joins the research staff of the National Bureau of Economic Research in New York, an affiliation that will run until 1981, and goes to work with Simon Kuznets on what doctors, lawyers and dentists earn. He lectures at Columbia in the same years. In 1938 he marries Rose Director, six years after the seating chart, and the partnership that begins here ends only at his death. Where the wedding took place is not recorded in anything that could be reached. No city, no synagogue, no date beyond the year.
suggested_refs: Simon Kuznets and Milton Friedman, Income from Independent Professional Practice, begun at the NBER in these years
sources: Online Archive of California, finding aid to the Milton Friedman papers 1931-2006

stops.name: Madison, the appointment that is not renewed
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1940 Wisconsin appointment and its brief tenure amid departmental controversy (Wikipedia; Hoover/OAC finding aid). Month set to September for the academic year. The internal politics of the department are reported in outline only; no faculty minutes were reached.
stops.campa: Wisconsin takes him as a visiting professor for a year and does not keep him. The department splits over the appointment, and the professional income research he is doing with Kuznets has made enemies well outside Madison. He tells the story afterward as a man cut down by campus politics, without much elaboration. The appointment simply lapses. He leaves university teaching for the duration of the war, and the manuscript that caused half the trouble stays unpublished until 1945.
suggested_refs: The University of Wisconsin economics department controversy of 1940-1941
sources: Online Archive of California, finding aid to the Milton Friedman papers 1931-2006

stops.name: The Treasury Building, Washington, the withholding tax
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1941-1943 Treasury service on wartime taxation and for his part in developing income tax withholding (Wikipedia; Hoover/OAC finding aid). Month set to September to order the segment. Coordinates are the historic Treasury Building per Wikipedia; his own office within the wartime bureaucracy is not established.
stops.campa: At the Treasury he works on how to pay for a war without inflating the currency, and helps design and argue for current withholding: the tax taken at the source, week by week, out of every wage in the country before the worker sees it. It is enacted in 1943 and it collects. For the rest of his life he says three things about it and never separates them: that withholding is what made a permanently large peacetime federal government affordable, that he would not build it a second time, and that he does not regret building it in a war.
suggested_refs: The Current Tax Payment Act of 1943, and Friedman's later published misgivings about withholding
sources: Online Archive of California, finding aid to the Milton Friedman papers 1931-2006

stops.name: Columbia University, the Statistical Research Group
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1943-1945 membership and for the group's weapons, metallurgy and quality control work (Wikipedia; Hoover/OAC finding aid gives him as associate director from 1943). Month defaulted to January to order the segment.
stops.campa: The Statistical Research Group, a war unit run out of Columbia, puts mathematical statisticians onto weapons design, alloy metallurgy and the sampling inspection of munitions. Wallis, whom he first met as a graduate student in Chicago, directs it. Abraham Wald and Frederick Mosteller work in the same rooms, and sequential analysis is invented inside them. Friedman is associate director at thirty-one, doing applied mathematics for the United States Army. He still has no doctorate, and will not have one for another three years.
suggested_refs: The Statistical Research Group, Columbia University, 1942-1945
sources: Online Archive of California, finding aid to the Milton Friedman papers 1931-2006

stops.name: University of Minnesota, the year before Chicago
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1945-1946 year at Minnesota as associate professor (Wikipedia; Hoover/OAC finding aid), and for the 1945 publication of Income from Independent Professional Practice after NBER delay (Econlib).
stops.campa: He teaches the 1945-46 academic year at Minnesota, with Stigler on the same faculty. In the spring Chicago writes to him about a post. Income from Independent Professional Practice, the Kuznets study that has trailed him since 1937, is published this year at last, after long resistance at the Bureau over what its findings said about the professions and their control of entry. It is the work his doctorate will rest on. He is thirty-three, has been a working economist for a decade, and has never held a permanent academic post.
suggested_refs: Milton Friedman and Simon Kuznets, Income from Independent Professional Practice (NBER, 1945)
sources: Online Archive of California, finding aid to the Milton Friedman papers 1931-2006

stops.name: Columbia University, the doctorate at last
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1946 Columbia Ph.D. (Wikipedia; Hoover/OAC finding aid). Month set to June for the degree season; the exact conferral date is not established.
stops.campa: Columbia awards the doctorate thirteen years after the fellowship year with Hotelling and Mitchell. The dissertation is the professional income study, and the degree had to wait on the book, because the Bureau's board balked at printing it. The delay has cost him a Wisconsin appointment and the better part of a decade of academic standing. What he takes out of it is not a grievance about the Bureau but a permanent suspicion of any institution placed where it can sit on a measurement it dislikes. He is thirty-three, and it is June.
suggested_refs: The National Bureau of Economic Research board's delay of the Friedman and Kuznets manuscript, 1941-1945
sources: Online Archive of California, finding aid to the Milton Friedman papers 1931-2006

stops.name: University of Chicago, the department he will make
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1946 appointment as associate professor and the tenure running to 1977 (Wikipedia; Hoover/OAC finding aid). The Aaron Director episode with The Road to Serfdom is dated 1943-1944 in friedrich_hayek.journey.json and is embedded here as a prior event, not as a scene of Friedman's.
stops.campa: Chicago hires him as associate professor of economics and he begins the price theory course he will teach for three decades. Aaron Director, his wife's brother, is already in the university; two years earlier Director had pressed Friedrich Hayek's The Road to Serfdom on the University of Chicago Press after three American publishers turned it down. The department Friedman joins is not yet the Chicago school. It becomes one across twenty years of seminars run by him, Stigler and Director, and what they build is a training system before it is a doctrine.
stops.quote: the most brilliant intellect in economics
stops.quote_source: Phrase quoted in Wikipedia, 'Milton Friedman'; the speaker is not identified in the fetched text
suggested_refs: Aaron Director's intervention with the University of Chicago Press over The Road to Serfdom, 1943-1944

sources: Online Archive of California, finding aid to the Milton Friedman papers 1931-2006

stops.name: Hotel du Parc, Mont Pelerin, the founding meeting
stops.date_confidence: attested for the date, the venue and Hayek's convening of thirty-nine scholars (Wikipedia, 'Mont Pelerin Society'; PBS Commanding Heights). Coordinate inherited byte-identical from friedrich_hayek.journey.json and ludwig_von_mises.journey.json, which use the same pin for the same meeting. The Mises walkout is Friedman's own recollection decades later, given through the Hoover Institution, and is not a verified 1947 transcript.
stops.campa: Thirty-nine scholars come up the mountain above Vevey to the Hotel du Parc, at Friedrich Hayek's invitation, to see whether liberalism can be rebuilt after the war that appeared to bury it. Friedman is thirty-four and among the youngest in the room. Ludwig von Mises is there, and Karl Popper, and Stigler, and Frank Knight. The story Friedman tells for the rest of his life is of Mises rising during a session on income distribution, calling the entire company a bunch of socialists, and walking out. It is his memory, told decades later. No transcript confirms it.
suggested_refs: ludwig_von_mises.journey.json
friedrich_hayek.journey.json
The Mont Pelerin Society statement of aims, 10 April 1947
sources: PBS, Commanding Heights, Milton Friedman biographical page

stops.name: University of Chicago, the workshop and the medal
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1948 promotion to full professor (Hoover/OAC finding aid), for the 1951 John Bates Clark Medal (Econlib; PBS Commanding Heights) and for the 1957 publication of A Theory of the Consumption Function (Wikipedia; Econlib). The medal's award city is not established anywhere reached, so the three events are gathered at his working pin and dated to the promotion.
stops.campa: He is made full professor at thirty-six and starts the Workshop in Money and Banking, where a student brings unfinished work to a table and has it taken apart in public, week after week, by him and by everyone else sitting there. In 1951 the American Economic Association gives him the John Bates Clark Medal. In 1957 comes A Theory of the Consumption Function, arguing that households spend against expected lifetime income rather than against this week's pay packet. The Keynesian multiplier depends on the opposite assumption.
suggested_refs: The Workshop in Money and Banking, University of Chicago
Milton Friedman, A Theory of the Consumption Function (1957)
sources: Online Archive of California, finding aid to the Milton Friedman papers 1931-2006
PBS, Commanding Heights, Milton Friedman biographical page

stops.name: Gonville and Caius College, Cambridge, in the other camp's house
stops.date_confidence: attested as the 1954-1955 academic year as Fulbright Visiting Fellow at Gonville and Caius (Wikipedia, verbatim). The verified pool's geography lens had given 1953-1954 and flagged a discrepancy; the discrepancy dissolves in favor of 1954-1955, which the chronology lens also carries. Month set to October for the Michaelmas term.
stops.campa: A Fulbright fellowship puts him for the year into Gonville and Caius, inside a faculty John Maynard Keynes had left eight years dead and which is now divided between his heirs and their opponents. Both camps want the visiting American, for opposite reasons. He argues at seminars and at table in the house where the theory he is attacking was built, and he is treated less as a guest than as an exhibit. The permanent income work is finished in this period. He goes home to Chicago in the summer of 1955.
suggested_refs: Gonville and Caius College, Cambridge, and the divided Cambridge faculty of the mid-1950s
john_maynard_keynes.journey.json

stops.name: Wabash College, Crawfordsville, the lectures that become a book
stops.date_confidence: attested that Capitalism and Freedom drew on lectures delivered in June 1956 at Wabash College (Wikipedia, 'Capitalism and Freedom'), with coordinates from Wikipedia's Wabash College article. The verified pool's geography lens had wrongly placed these lectures at the University of Chicago and framed them as a return from sabbatical; both are corrected here. The William Volker Fund financing is carried from dossier material and was not independently re-verified.
stops.campa: At a summer institute at Wabash College in Crawfordsville, Indiana, financed through the William Volker Fund's network, he delivers the lectures that will become Capitalism and Freedom. The audience is small and the setting is a men's liberal arts college surrounded by corn. Rose takes the transcripts afterward and works them into a book across six years, cutting, reordering and rewriting until an argument spoken aloud holds together as prose. The 1962 volume carries his name alone on the cover.
suggested_refs: The William Volker Fund summer institutes of the 1950s
Milton Friedman, Capitalism and Freedom (University of Chicago Press, 1962)

segments.name: The Doctrine in Print and on Commission

stops.name: University of Chicago, Capitalism and Freedom
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1962 publication by the University of Chicago Press, for sales past half a million copies and eighteen translations, and for the later listings by Time and National Review (Wikipedia, 'Capitalism and Freedom'). Month defaulted to January to order the segment.
stops.campa: The University of Chicago Press publishes Capitalism and Freedom. Inside it are a volunteer army, floating exchange rates, a negative income tax, the abolition of occupational licensing, and school vouchers: public money following the child to whatever school the parents pick. Almost none of it is respectable in 1962, and most of it is still being argued about sixty years later. It sells past half a million copies, goes into eighteen languages, and turns up decades on in Time's list of the hundred best nonfiction books in English since 1923 and in National Review's list too.
suggested_refs: Milton Friedman, Capitalism and Freedom (1962), and Rose Friedman's editorial hand in it

stops.name: New York, A Monetary History with Anna Schwartz
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1963 publication of A Monetary History of the United States, 1867-1960, co-authored with Anna Jacobson Schwartz (Wikipedia; Econlib). The verified pool places publication at Princeton; the pin here is the NBER in New York, where the work and Schwartz's series were housed, and the exact NBER address was not established. Month defaulted to January.
stops.campa: With Anna Jacobson Schwartz, who has been assembling the underlying series at the Bureau for years, he publishes A Monetary History of the United States, 1867-1960: ninety-three years of the money stock reconstructed and set beside everything that happened to the economy. The book rests on Schwartz's numbers as much as on his theory. Its chapter on 1929 to 1933 argues that the Federal Reserve turned a recession into the Great Depression by letting the quantity of money fall by a third, and the series is printed underneath the argument.
suggested_refs: Milton Friedman and Anna Jacobson Schwartz, A Monetary History of the United States, 1867-1960 (Princeton, 1963)

stops.name: Fairlee, Vermont, the cottage called Capitaf
stops.date_confidence: attested that the Friedmans built a Vermont cottage at Fairlee during the 1960s and kept it for decades (Wikipedia); the exact year is not established and 1965 is used only to order the segment. The name Capitaf and its derivation from Capitalism and Freedom are carried from dossier material and were not independently re-verified. Coordinates are the town, not the house.
stops.campa: They build a cottage in the hills above Fairlee and call it Capitaf, from the title of the book, capitalism and freedom run together into one word on a Vermont mailbox. Summers go here for the next forty years: students and colleagues drive up, arguments continue on a porch with no institution attached to them, and Rose runs the house. Nothing about the place is grand and nothing about it is public. The year it was built is not recorded in anything reachable, only the decade, and the coordinate is the town rather than the house.
suggested_refs: Capitaf, the Friedman cottage at Fairlee, Vermont

stops.name: American Economic Association, the presidency and the column
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1967 AEA presidency (PBS Commanding Heights; Econlib) and for the Newsweek column running from 1966 to 1984 (Wikipedia). The city of the 1967 annual meeting is not established in anything reached, so the stop sits at his Chicago base; December is used because the association meets at year's end.
stops.campa: The profession elects him its president, twenty-seven years after two departments declined to keep him. Since the year before he has been writing a column in Newsweek, a page in rotation with economists who disagree with him, and he keeps it up until 1984. That column is where the arguments leave the seminar room: several million people who will never open a journal read him every third week, in a magazine bought for something else. He is fifty-five years old.
suggested_refs: Friedman's Newsweek column, 1966-1984
sources: PBS, Commanding Heights, Milton Friedman biographical page

stops.name: Washington, the commission on the draft
stops.date_confidence: attested that Friedman served on President Nixon's Commission on an All-Volunteer Armed Force, the Gates Commission (PBS Commanding Heights confirms the Nixon advisory role; the commission dates come from dossier material corroborated only in outline). Month defaulted to January to order the segment.
stops.campa: Nixon appoints a commission to consider ending conscription and Friedman sits on it. His argument in the room is plain price theory: the draft is a tax in kind, collected from the young men least able to buy their way out of it, and an army raised by paying the going wage costs the nation less than an army raised by seizing labor at gunpoint. He is arguing this with men who have commanded armies, in the middle of a war that is drafting eighteen year olds while he speaks. The commission reports for abolition.
suggested_refs: The Report of the President's Commission on an All-Volunteer Armed Force (the Gates Commission), 1970
sources: PBS, Commanding Heights, Milton Friedman biographical page

stops.name: Mayo Clinic, Rochester, the bypass
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. Both the location and the Nixon remark come from family recollection reported in dossier material, which itself flags the joke as anecdotal rather than a transcript; no independent confirmation was obtained. The year is given as approximately his sixtieth and is used to order the segment.
stops.campa: Around his sixtieth year his heart fails him and he is opened for a coronary bypass at the Mayo Clinic in Rochester, a procedure that in 1972 is still new enough to be dangerous. He recovers and lives another thirty-four years. The family's account has the President telephoning afterward with a line about being relieved it was the heart rather than the brain. That comes down as recollection and not as a recording, and the year and the hospital arrive by the same uncertain route.
stops.quote: I was glad to hear it was your heart and not your brain.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Richard Nixon in a family recollection reported in Friedman dossier material; not a verbatim transcript
suggested_refs: The Friedman family recollections of the 1972 surgery
sources: Family/dossier recollection, unconfirmed against any independent source

stops.name: Santiago, the lectures on the fragility of freedom
stops.date_confidence: attested that Friedman and Arnold Harberger traveled to Chile in March 1975 at the invitation of a private Chilean institution and that Friedman lectured publicly (PBS Commanding Heights confirms the Chile contact; the visit's specifics rest on Edwards and Montes, Journal of the History of Economic Thought 42, 2020, which was not independently fetched, the JSTOR request having failed). The lecture text is fetched from the Hoover Institution's own reproduction. The specific hall is not identified; coordinates are central Santiago.
stops.campa: He comes to Santiago with Arnold Harberger at the invitation of a private Chilean institution, eighteen months after the coup, into a country with inflation running in the hundreds of percent and a government that imprisons and kills its opponents. He lectures in public on the fragility of freedom and on the welfare state as the attempt to do good at somebody else's expense. The men running the Chilean economy are his students and Harberger's, trained at Chicago under an exchange with the Catholic University that has been running since the 1950s.
stops.quote: Freedom is very far from being the natural state of mankind; on the contrary, it is an extraordinarily unusual situation.
stops.quote_source: Milton Friedman, The Fragility of Freedom, lecture text as reproduced at hoover.org/research/fragility-freedom
suggested_refs: The University of Chicago and Pontificia Universidad Catolica de Chile exchange that produced the Chicago Boys
Sebastian Edwards and Leonidas Montes, 'Milton Friedman in Chile', Journal of the History of Economic Thought 42 (2020)
sources: PBS, Commanding Heights, Milton Friedman biographical page

stops.name: Santiago, forty-five minutes with Pinochet
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction as to the exact date and the meeting's length, which come from dossier material citing Edwards and Montes and were not independently re-verified; the fact of Friedman's advisory contact with Pinochet's Chile is attested (PBS Commanding Heights). Coordinate inherited byte-identical from augusto_pinochet.journey.json, which uses this Santiago pin. Note that Pinochet's own file has no stop for this meeting: the episode is absent there.
stops.campa: He is taken to see Augusto Pinochet and the meeting runs about three quarters of an hour. He tells the general that Chile's inflation is the government's own doing, that the cure is to stop printing money and to stop fast rather than by degrees, and that a market economy would decentralize the power the state is currently holding in one fist. He asks nothing and is paid nothing. The junta will do roughly what he said. Nobody in the room puts a number on the unemployment it will take to do it.
stops.quote: The emphasis of that talk was that free markets would undermine political centralization and political control.
stops.quote_source: Milton Friedman, interview, PBS Commanding Heights transcript, 10/01/00
suggested_refs: augusto_pinochet.journey.json
Sebastian Edwards and Leonidas Montes on the Friedman visit and the Pinochet meeting

stops.name: Chicago, the letter of 21 April
stops.date_confidence: the letter's date of 21 April 1975 is attested (Wikipedia, 'Miracle of Chile'); its full text was not fetched this session and the account of its contents rests on the Friedmans' memoir as summarized by Edwards and Montes. The verified pool's geography lens pinned this to Santiago; since the letter was mailed rather than delivered, it is placed where it was written. The Letelier essay's title and venue come from dossier material, not from an independent fetch.
stops.campa: A month after the meeting he writes to Pinochet from Chicago and puts the advice on paper: shock treatment, a sharp cut in government spending, and beside it measures to relieve the people the adjustment will injure. Because it is a letter it survives, and it is later printed in the Friedmans' own memoir, which is why this episode cannot be argued in generalities. Orlando Letelier, Salvador Allende's ambassador in Washington, answers it the following year in The Nation, under the title The Chicago Boys in Chile: Economic Freedom's Awful Toll.
suggested_refs: Orlando Letelier, 'The Chicago Boys in Chile: Economic Freedom's Awful Toll', The Nation (1976)

stops.name: Stockholm Concert Hall, the prize and the letters against it
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1976 award and its citation wording (Wikipedia), for the protests, and for the four laureates who wrote to the New York Times in October 1976 (Wikipedia). Nobelprize.org was unreachable this session, so the ceremony venue rests on the Nobel Foundation's standard practice of awarding at the Stockholm Concert Hall on 10 December, corroborated by Wikipedia's Stockholm Concert Hall and Nobel Memorial Prize articles. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from friedrich_hayek.journey.json's 1974 Stockholm stop, the same venue and the same annual ceremony. The verified pool's attribution of the protest to Gunnar Myrdal is corrected: Myrdal's published position was that the economics prize should be abolished.
stops.campa: The Sveriges Riksbank Prize is given him for consumption analysis, monetary history and theory, and for his demonstration of the complexity of stabilisation policy. Outside there are demonstrators, and the reason is Chile rather than the money supply. Four Nobel laureates, George Wald, Linus Pauling, David Baltimore and Salvador Luria, had already written to the New York Times in October to protest the award. Friedman, looking out at the pickets, recognizes faces he has seen outside his lectures in Chicago and in Santiago. He takes the prize at the Concert Hall on 10 December.
stops.quote: I remember seeing the same faces in the crowd in a talk in Chicago and a talk in Santiago. And there was no doubt that there was a concerted effort to tar and feather me.
stops.quote_source: Milton Friedman, interview, PBS Commanding Heights transcript, 10/01/00

segments.name: The Move West and the Broadcast

stops.name: Russian Hill, San Francisco, the apartment above the bay
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1977 retirement from Chicago, the move to San Francisco, the Russian Hill apartment held until his death, and the visiting scholar post at the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco (Wikipedia). Month set to June to order the segment; the exact month of the move is not established.
stops.campa: At sixty-five he retires from Chicago after thirty-one years and moves with Rose into an apartment on Russian Hill, high over the bay, which is home for the rest of his life. He takes a visiting scholar's post at the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco: the economist who spent his career arguing that the Federal Reserve turned a downturn into the Great Depression now keeps a desk in one of its buildings. Neither side appears to find this strange. He will not teach a university course again.
suggested_refs: The Friedmans' Russian Hill apartment, San Francisco, 1977-2006

stops.name: Hoover Institution, Stanford, the last post
stops.date_confidence: attested for the Hoover Institution senior research fellowship from 1977 until his death (Wikipedia; Hoover/OAC finding aid gives the Hoover appointment from 1977). Month set to September for the academic year.
stops.campa: Stanford's Hoover Institution takes him as senior research fellow and he holds the post for the last twenty-nine years of his life. The work here is not the seminar work of Hyde Park. It is testimony, columns, television, foreign advising, and a running argument with people who now actually govern. Hoover will also become where the paper lands: two hundred and twenty-seven manuscript boxes, roughly a hundred linear feet of correspondence, drafts, photographs and film.
suggested_refs: The Milton Friedman papers, 1931-2006, Hoover Institution Library and Archives
sources: Online Archive of California, finding aid to the Milton Friedman papers 1931-2006

stops.name: San Francisco, Free to Choose goes out on television
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1980 PBS series in ten episodes with the companion book written with Rose, for the book topping the American bestseller list for five weeks, for translation into roughly two dozen languages, and for the 1990 update (Wikipedia, 'Free to Choose'; Econlib). The series has no single production site; the pin is his San Francisco base and the month is defaulted to January.
stops.campa: Free to Choose goes out on public television in ten episodes. Half of each hour is filmed argument in the field, and half is Friedman sitting at a table being contradicted by people who think he is wrong. The companion book, written with Rose, tops the American bestseller list for five weeks and is translated into some two dozen languages. The series is remade in 1990. He spent thirty years persuading economists; the audience for this is anyone with a television, and he is sixty-seven when the first episode airs.
stops.quote: If present public expenditure were made available to parents regardless of where they send their children, a wide variety of schools would spring up to meet the demand.
stops.quote_source: Milton Friedman, 'Free to Choose', Hoover Digest 2005 no. 3, hoover.org/research/free-choose
suggested_refs: Milton and Rose Friedman, Free to Choose (Harcourt, 1980) and the ten-part PBS series
sources: Milton Friedman, 'Free to Choose', Hoover Digest 2005 no. 3 (hoover.org)

stops.name: Beijing, the first China trip
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction as to the year and the lecture context, which come from dossier material; that Friedman visited China and advised governments there is attested in general (Wikipedia), but the 1980 date specifically was not independently re-verified. Month set to September to order the segment; coordinates are central Beijing, no venue established.
stops.campa: He goes to China for the first time and lectures under official auspices, two years into the reform period, to rooms of officials for whom the vocabulary of prices and markets is both new and politically dangerous to be caught using. He is told what the plan requires. He answers with what prices do. The country he is standing in has spent thirty years abolishing the thing he has spent thirty years explaining. What he actually said in those rooms is not preserved in anything reachable, and even the year rests on secondary report rather than on a document.
suggested_refs: Friedman's three visits to China, 1980, 1988 and 1993
sources: Dossier travel summary, not independently verified for the 1980 date

stops.name: Santiago, the second meeting nobody notices
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The second Chile visit and second Pinochet meeting of November 1981 are reported by archival research by Sebastian Edwards and Leonidas Montes as summarized in dossier material; neither was independently re-fetched this session. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from augusto_pinochet.journey.json. Day defaulted to the first of the month.
stops.campa: He returns to Chile and meets Pinochet a second time, six years after the first, in a visit that attracts almost no attention while it is happening. The peso is pegged to the dollar, the banks are lending against the peg, and Friedman thinks the arrangement is wrong: a fixed exchange rate is not the instrument for this, and he says so. Within months the peg breaks and the Chilean banking system collapses into the worst crisis of the whole military period. The record of the visit rests on archival work published decades later.
suggested_refs: augusto_pinochet.journey.json
Sebastian Edwards and Leonidas Montes on Friedman's second Chilean visit
sources: Dossier synthesis of Edwards and Montes scholarship, not independently re-fetched

stops.name: Reykjavik, the lecture and the televised debate
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, and a weak one. The 1984 Iceland lecture and television debate come from a dossier travel summary that cites no primary source, and nothing corroborating was reachable this session. Month and day defaulted to January to order the segment.
stops.campa: He lectures in Reykjavik and takes part in a televised debate, in a small North Atlantic economy that is fished, subsidized and heavily directed from the center. The trip is carried here on secondary report alone. No primary source for it could be reached: not a transcript, not a broadcast date, not the name of whoever sat across from him at the table. It is in the record because his own travel summaries put it there. Somebody in Reykjavik in 1984 argued with Milton Friedman on television, and nothing reachable says who.
suggested_refs: Icelandic broadcast archives for 1984, not consulted

stops.name: Beijing, two hours with Zhao Ziyang
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction as to place. The 1988 conference visit and the long meeting with Communist Party general secretary Zhao Ziyang are widely reported in the historiography of Chinese reform as summarized in dossier material, but no source confirming Zhongnanhai as the site was fetched; the building is inference from where Chinese leaders customarily receive foreign visitors. Month set to September to order the segment.
stops.campa: At a conference in Beijing he is received by Zhao Ziyang, general secretary of the Communist Party, and they talk for nearly two hours. Friedman argues for freeing prices quickly rather than in stages, on the ground that a half-freed price system gives every good two prices and turns the economy into an arbitrage machine. Zhao's factional enemies inside the Party will later use the meeting against him, as evidence of contamination by extreme liberal foreign ideas. Which building they sat in is a guess.
suggested_refs: Chinese reform historiography on Zhao Ziyang's foreign economic advisers, 1988
sources: Dossier summary of the 1988 Zhao Ziyang meeting, location unconfirmed

stops.name: The White House, the East Room, the Medal of Freedom
stops.date_confidence: attested for the Presidential Medal of Freedom and the National Medal of Science in 1988 (Wikipedia; Hoover/OAC finding aid), with the East Room location corroborated by a photo caption in Wikipedia's Milton Friedman article and the 17 October date carried from dossier material.
stops.campa: Reagan puts the Presidential Medal of Freedom around his neck in the East Room, before an audience of officials of the government whose size Friedman has spent forty years arguing against. The citation praises the technical economics and the moral case for economic freedom in the same breath, which is how he has always insisted the two be taken. The National Medal of Science arrives the same year. He is seventy-six and has been out of a university department for eleven of those years.
suggested_refs: The Presidential Medal of Freedom citation, 17 October 1988
sources: Online Archive of California, finding aid to the Milton Friedman papers 1931-2006

stops.name: Beijing, the third trip and the doubt
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The 1993 meeting with Communist Party general secretary Jiang Zemin comes from a dossier summary with no primary citation and was not independently confirmed; the continued China engagement is consistent with the attested 1980 and 1988 trips. Month and day defaulted to January.
stops.campa: His third trip to China takes him to Jiang Zemin, general secretary now in Zhao Ziyang's place. He comes away less convinced than he was in 1988: the reform vocabulary has become fluent, and the willingness to actually surrender control over prices and enterprises does not match the fluency. He is eighty years old and has by now made the same argument in Santiago, in Reykjavik and twice in Beijing. No primary account of this meeting was reachable, only secondary summaries of it.
suggested_refs: Friedman's published reflections on the pace of Chinese reform after 1993

stops.name: Indianapolis, the foundation for educational choice
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1996 founding of the Friedman Foundation for Educational Choice and for the 2016 renaming to EdChoice (Wikipedia). The stated reason for the rename is corrected here to the sourced one: EdChoice's own account of the Friedmans' wish to separate their personal legacy from the intellectual legacy of educational choice. Indianapolis is inference from the organization's later headquarters; no source reached fixes the founding city. Month and day defaulted to January.
stops.campa: He and Rose put their name and their money behind a foundation for educational choice, giving the voucher proposal from Capitalism and Freedom an institution thirty-four years after the book. It is what he wants his name on at eighty-four. In 2016 the foundation renames itself EdChoice, on its own account because the Friedmans had wished their personal legacy kept separate from the intellectual legacy of educational choice. Where the founding papers were actually signed is not established here.
suggested_refs: EdChoice, formerly the Milton and Rose D. Friedman Foundation for Educational Choice

stops.name: Chicago, the long interview about the century
stops.date_confidence: attested. The PBS Commanding Heights interview transcript is dated 10/01/00 and was fetched directly (pbs.org/wgbh/commandingheights). The verified pool's quotations of it were not verbatim and are corrected here against the transcript text.
stops.campa: He sits for a long television interview about the century's economic argument, and Chile comes up as it always does. His account is that the intellectual community was on Salvador Allende's side rather than Pinochet's, and that they regarded him as a traitor for having been willing to talk in Chile at all. His defense is not that the economics was pleasant. It is that the junta was eventually replaced by a democracy and that free markets did the work of getting the country there.
stops.quote: Most of the intellectual community, the intellectual elite, as it were, were on the side of Allende, not on the side of Pinochet... in a sense they regarded me as a traitor for having been willing to talk in Chile.
stops.quote_source: Milton Friedman, interview, PBS Commanding Heights transcript, 10/01/00

stops.name: San Francisco, heart failure at ninety-four
stops.date_confidence: attested for the date, the cause and the age (Wikipedia infobox, fetched directly); the hospital is not named in any source reached. The absence of a recorded resting place is a documented gap rather than a finding: Wikipedia's infobox, which normally carries a resting place field, leaves it empty for Friedman, and no cemetery record was reachable. That absence is not proof of anything.
stops.campa: He dies of heart failure at ninety-four, having been taken to a hospital near the Russian Hill apartment. He was writing and giving interviews nearly to the end. The hospital is not named in any source that could be reached. Neither is a grave: the reference entry that would ordinarily record a resting place leaves the line blank, and no cemetery register turned up. It may mean cremation without a marker. It may only mean that nobody wrote it down.
suggested_refs: The gap in the record concerning Friedman's burial or cremation
sources: Find a Grave searches, blocked or empty this session

stops.name: University of Chicago, the institute that had to be renamed
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 2008 founding of the Milton Friedman Institute with a two hundred million dollar commitment, for the protest letter signed by more than 170 faculty, and for the June 2011 merger with the Becker Center into the Becker Friedman Institute (Wikipedia, 'Milton Friedman Institute'). Month and day defaulted to January.
stops.campa: Two years after his death the University of Chicago announces a Milton Friedman Institute for Research in Economics, two hundred million dollars behind it, intended by its president to make the university the primary intellectual destination for economics. More than a hundred and seventy of its own faculty sign a letter of protest: putting that name on a research institute reads as the university endorsing a politics. In June 2011 the institute merges with the Becker Center and becomes the Becker Friedman Institute, with Gary Becker's name standing in front of his.
suggested_refs: The 2008 University of Chicago faculty letter opposing the Milton Friedman Institute

stops.name: Hoover Institution, Stanford, two hundred and twenty-seven boxes
stops.date_confidence: attested for the collection's size and contents, for research access from 1977 with increments through 2008, and for the digitized distribution via the Collected Works project (Online Archive of California finding aid, fetched). The 2008 date marks the last increment; month defaulted to June.
stops.campa: The paper settles at Hoover: two hundred and twenty-seven manuscript boxes, roughly a hundred linear feet of speeches, correspondence, manuscripts, photographs and audio and video, open to researchers from 1977 and still taking in material as late as 2008. The recordings are digitized and issued as the Collected Works, so that the voice goes on arguing after the man has stopped. The finding aid that governs the whole collection opens with a chronology of his life. The chronology runs to eleven lines.
suggested_refs: The Collected Works of Milton Friedman project, Hoover Institution
sources: Online Archive of California, finding aid to the Milton Friedman papers 1931-2006 (oac.cdlib.org/findaid/ark:/13030/tf7t1nb2hx/)

stops.name: Santiago, the phrase that will not die
stops.date_confidence: attested that the term Chicago Boys persists in Chilean public discourse and that a Chilean documentary film titled Chicago Boys appeared in 2015 (Wikipedia, 'Chicago Boys'); a dedicated fetch on the film's own page returned 404, so its director and reception are not stated. The Klein and Norberg material is attested (Wikipedia, 'The Shock Doctrine'). Month and day defaulted to January.
stops.campa: In Chile the phrase stays in the language. Chicago Boys is what the newspapers and the kitchens call what was done to the economy under the dictatorship and the men who did it, and a documentary released in 2015 takes the words as its title without needing to explain them. Naomi Klein had made Friedman the emblem of a global disaster capitalism in 2007; Johan Norberg of the Cato Institute answered that the portrait was a straw man, hopelessly flawed at virtually every level. Neither reading has displaced the other, and the phrase in the newspapers and the kitchens belongs to neither of them.
suggested_refs: Naomi Klein, The Shock Doctrine (2007), and Johan Norberg's published rebuttal
Chicago Boys (documentary film, Chile, 2015)
